title: Revealing the Gap in Human and VLM Scene Description through Counterfactual Semantic Saliency
claim: Black-box ablation of objects exposes that model-derived object importance diverges from human-derived importance, a gap seen across most evaluated models.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right; stacked model and human rows, red mismatch arrow, density plot
description: The figure reads left to right. The first panel stacks a factual photo of an egret on a dock with two counterfactual versions. Each has a different object ablated, marked by a red box. Two arrows lead to rounded boxes. The top box has model icons (n=19) and gray text bubbles with the models' descriptions of each scene. The bottom box has a human-participants icon and their descriptions. A red dashed outline marks the description that shifted most. Each row produces a heatmap of the dock scene, with a blue-to-red scale from min to max importance. The egret is highlighted for models and the trash for humans, and a red double arrow with bold 'Mismatch!' sits between them. The rightmost panel is a blue density curve of the percentage of VLMs mismatched to humans, with scene thumbnails scattered over it.
caption: Counterfactual Semantic Saliency (CSS) reveals a pervasive scene comprehension gap between humans and vision-language models (VLMs). CSS quantifies the importance of an object by ablating it from a factual scene and measuring the semantic shift in the resulting descriptions. The object causing the maximal semantic shift is considered the most critical to scene perception. The example illustrates a mismatch between ALL 19 models and humans. The rightmost plot illustrates the percentage of the evaluated VLMs that failed to identify the human-consensus critical object for a given scene.
abstract: Evaluating whether large vision-language models (VLMs) align with human perception for high-level semantic scene comprehension remains a challenge. Traditional white-box interpretability methods are inapplicable to closed-source architectures and passive metrics fail to isolate causal features. We introduce Counterfactual Semantic Saliency (CSS). This black-box, model-agnostic framework quantifies the importance of objects by measuring the semantic shift induced by their causal ablation from a scene. To evaluate AI-human semantic alignment, we tested prominent VLMs against a human psychophysics baseline comprising 16,603 valid responses across 307 complex natural scenes and 1,306 high-fidelity counterfactual variants. Our analysis reveals a pervasive scene comprehension gap: models exhibit an over-reliance (relative to humans) on object size, object centrality, and low-level saliency of objects. In contrast, models are less sensitive to the presence of people in the scenes than our human participants when describing the images. The over-reliance on object size is a primary driver explaining variations in model-human semantic divergence. Code and data are available at https://github.com/starsky77/Counterfactual-Semantic-Saliency-Data .
